Issued at 152 AM EDT Sat Aug 1 2026

             -----------Synoptic Overview-----------

Early this morning, water vapor imagery reveals a rather complex
upper-air pattern across the U.S. for the first day of August. A
pair of shortwaves is keeping a broad dip in the jet stream over
the Eastern U.S. The stronger of these two features is currently
located near the Quad Cities. Exceptionally stout ridging extends
from the Caribbean to the Desert Southwest, where 01/00Z RAOBs
returned H5 heights of 601 dam at Flagstaff, AZ and 600 dam at
El Paso, TX. Locally, H5 heights exceed 590 dam; warm mid-level
temperatures are resulting in poor H7-H5 lapse rates, which is
rather typical for the time of year.

The energy approaching the Mississippi Valley will soon carve out a 
longwave trough; it will then move little through Sunday. A weak 
quasi-stationary front should remain well north of Central Florida. 
Mean southwesterly flow in the boundary layer maintains rich 
moisture over the state with PWAT values from 100-130% of normal 
through at least Monday. Amid subtle height falls, weak vorticity 
maxima are forecast to rotate around the trough west of Florida, 
providing forcing for occasional convection.

By Monday, the Bermuda High will attempt to retrograde over the
W Atlantic, promoting height rises over Florida. As ensemble
members weaken the trough over the Tennessee Valley by Tuesday,
the near-surface ridge axis is likely to trek north of our latitude
by midweek, providing light onshore flow off the Atlantic.

Confidence trails off late in the work week and toward next
weekend. The 31/12Z grand ensemble and fellow AI members initialized
an easterly wave over the Canary Islands. The model suite sends
this disturbance westward across the Atlantic, perhaps approaching
Florida by late Thursday or Friday. PWAT anomalies clearly show an
increase in moisture associated with this feature, but we expect 
further refinements to the forecast as this disturbance is currently 
3800 miles to our east.

             -------Sensible Weather & Impacts-------

This Weekend...

Periods of active weather should be expected. Those planning to
be outdoors will need to listen for thunder, watch for darkening
skies, and find safe shelter when storms threaten!

Nocturnal showers and storms extending along the FL Panhandle early
this morning suggest a weak disturbance is present. If this is the
case, an earlier-than-normal start to showers and storms is on the
table for today, perhaps as early as late morning/midday near and
northwest of Interstate 4. Relatively weak offshore winds may allow 
a sea breeze to form and hug the coast. Boundary interactions would 
support numerous storms near and east of I-95 in the afternoon. Wind 
gusts to 40-45 mph and frequent lightning will be the primary 
hazards. There is a 5-10% chance of rainfall totals exceeding 3", 
especially along the coast. Localized urban flooding is possible 
where this rainfall occurs over poorly drained areas.

Boundary-layer flow increases from Saturday night into Sunday. 
Additional weak energy approaching N FL is likely to spark 
overnight showers and storms northwest of our area, and some of 
this may reach Lake County overnight. This portends another early 
start to shower and storm chances on Sunday, especially over our 
northern half. Then, daytime heating will provide an additional 
spark for storm development over the eastern half of the 
peninsula. While shear is weak, the enhanced mid-level flow (20-25
kts) will be sufficient for a few stronger storms with wind gusts
from 50 to 55 mph. There is a very small chance for a severe gust
to around 60 mph.

Hot and muggy conditions continue, with highs in the low/mid 90s
and heat indices from 100 to 107. Of the two days, today looks
slightly hotter.

Monday - Tuesday...

This still appears to be a transition period for local weather
conditions. High pressure will begin to push overhead, weakening
background flow just a bit. As that occurs, the sea breeze will
begin to move inland each afternoon, with better progression
especially by Tuesday. Near- to above-normal moisture values will
continue to support scattered to numerous showers and storms (50%
to 80%) each day. Seasonably hot temperatures will persist as well,
outside of the storms.

Wednesday - next Saturday...

On Wednesday and Thursday, light onshore flow should finally return,
giving us more typical summertime conditions. As the sea breeze
pushes inland, a few storms may try to form closer to the coast
before concentrating over the interior and points westward.

By Friday and Saturday, the easterly wave mentioned in the overview 
may reach the state. Should this happen, it would provide increased 
moisture and an uptick in shower/storm opportunities late in the 
week. While a few deterministic runs have recently shown tropical 
development with this feature, the GEFS and EPS ensembles are 
generally unimpressed and favor an open wave/trough as it passes
